clue.text: Light entertainment on a sound basis

definitions.text: Light entertainment on a sound basis

parts.words: Light entertainment on a sound basis
parts.note: read literally: a show made of floodlighting backed by a recorded soundtrack, staged at a historic building after dark

explanation.surface: A gentle evening show that depends on good audio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light entertainment' usually means comedy or variety; here it is entertainment made of light, and 'sound basis' is a soundtrack rather than a firm footing.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase names an outdoor night spectacle where floodlit monuments are narrated by recorded music and voices.

clue.text: Well-turned phrases of the mountaineers

indicators.note: turned means the letters are turned about into a new order, an anagram signal

explanation.surface: Elegantly crafted sayings of climbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well-turned' looks like praise for elegant phrasing; it rearranges PHRASES.
explanation.definitionFit: The Himalayan people famed as guides and porters on Everest expeditions are climbers themselves.

clue.text: Date one between Poles

indicators.note: between places the word one inside, flanked by the two poles

parts.note: N and S are the north and south poles

explanation.surface: A romantic date with someone sitting between two Polish people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' are not Polish people but the North and South poles, N and S, with ONE between them.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar the ninth day before the Ides is a fixed day of the month.

clue.text: Holmes's breakfast-time causerie?

parts.note: Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, informal conversation over the morning meal

explanation.surface: What Sherlock Holmes chatted about over breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: Holmes is not Sherlock but Oliver Wendell Holmes, author of The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table; a causerie is an informal chat.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal conversation over a meal, as in the collected sayings of a host at dinner, is a chatty genre.

clue.text: Top lousy egg — that's one thing.

parts.note: U stands for upper-class, the top social class
a nit is the egg of a louse

explanation.surface: An awful egg is just one item on the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lousy' is not 'bad' but 'of a louse'; U is the old label for upper-class usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A single item, a complete whole counted as one, is a synonym for a single thing.

clue.text: They don't appreciate one strange turn

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: turn means the letters of strange are turned into a different order

explanation.surface: People who don't value a kind but odd favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange turn' looks like an odd good deed; 'turn' rearranges STRANGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ungrateful people are those who fail to show thanks for kindness.

clue.text: "Such as are of —— Years"

parts.note: the Book of Common Prayer has a baptism service for those of more mature age, adults rather than infants

explanation.surface: A line quoted from the Prayer Book with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The Book of Common Prayer's adult baptism service is titled 'The Ministration of Baptism to such as are of Riper Years'.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of a word meaning mature fills the gap in the Prayer Book title.

clue.text: Circassian stage aunt not so hot ?

parts.note: Auntie Mame is the title heroine of a stage play and musical about an eccentric aunt
luke is an old word for tepid, surviving in lukewarm

explanation.surface: A theatrical aunt from the Caucasus who is a bit cool.
explanation.walkthrough: Auntie Mame is the stage aunt; LUKE is lukewarm without the 'warm'. The Mameluke soldier-slaves of Egypt were largely Circassian.
explanation.definitionFit: The slave-soldiers who ruled medieval Egypt were drawn largely from Circassians of the Caucasus.

clue.text: R.A.F. officer's ready for a drink.

parts.note: PO is a Pilot Officer in the Royal Air Force; with the 's this gives POS
set means ready, as in 'ready, steady, go'

explanation.surface: An air force officer is keen for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ready for' is a link in the surface but splits into SET plus 'for'; the 's of 'officer's' stays as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An old hot beverage of milk curdled with ale or wine is a kind of drink.

clue.text: Preparing one for an appearance with Burke ?

definitions.text: Preparing one for an appearance with Burke ?

parts.words: Preparing one for an appearance with Burke ?
parts.note: Burke's Peerage lists the titled families of Britain, so to appear in it one must first be raised to the peerage

explanation.surface: Getting someone ready to meet a person called Burke.
explanation.walkthrough: Burke is not a person to meet but Burke's Peerage, the reference book of the British aristocracy.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising someone to a title of nobility is what qualifies a family for an entry in that peerage directory.

clue.text: Burlington House V.I.P. has a party in the Gallery

parts.note: Burlington House in London is home of the Royal Academy, whose head is the PRA, President of the Royal Academy
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: The head of the Royal Academy throws a party in an art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: Burlington House is the London building on Piccadilly that houses the Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: The Prado in Madrid is one of the world's great national art museums.

clue.text: One who dispatches the bill.

definitions.meaning: someone who posts letters or sends things off
a bill is a printed notice stuck up on a wall

explanation.definitionFit: A sender is literally one who posts; a placard or bill stuck on a hoarding is the other sense.

clue.text: Justice in beautiful but monstrous setting.

parts.note: fair is an old word for beautiful
Loch Ness in Scotland is the setting of the legendary Loch Ness Monster

explanation.surface: Justice placed in a lovely yet grotesque backdrop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'monstrous setting' is Loch Ness, home of the fabled monster 'Nessie'.
explanation.definitionFit: Even-handed treatment, the quality a just judge shows, is a synonym of justice.

clue.text: Punch had an able one

parts.note: Sir Owen ... was the long-serving editor of the humorous magazine Punch, and an able sailor rank in the Royal Navy shares his surname

explanation.surface: The puppet Punch had a capable assistant.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch is the British satirical magazine, edited 1906-32 by Owen Seaman; 'able one' recalls the naval rank of able seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailor is the everyday meaning, and the rank 'able' completes the naval phrase; Punch's editor bore the same name.

clue.text: Part cattle county

definitions.meaning: half of the name of the Scottish beef breed ... Angus
a former Scottish shire in the north-east

explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish city lends its name to the first half of a beef breed and to a former shire.

clue.text: Smallest water-pipe ?

parts.note: the tiniest channel carrying water is in the body: the duct draining tears from the eye

explanation.surface: Asking for the narrowest plumbing pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: The plumbing picture misleads; the water is tears and the pipe is in the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The canal from the eye to the nose carries away lachrymal fluid, a minute natural conduit.

clue.text: It's intended to give you the pip!

definitions.text: It's intended to give you the pip!

parts.words: It's intended to give you the pip!
parts.note: a rude noise made with the tongue is meant to annoy, give someone the pip, and the soft fruit is full of pips

explanation.surface: Something designed purely to irritate you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give you the pip' is British slang for annoy; the jeering noise blown with the tongue does that, and the fruit literally gives pips.
explanation.definitionFit: Blowing a derisive noise with the lips annoys its target, and the berry of the same name contains seeds.

clue.text: Change course when in distress

definitions.meaning: a nautical term: to turn a ship onto the opposite tack
upset or troubled, as in 'very put out'

explanation.definitionFit: Sailors use the phrase for turning onto another heading; in British speech it also means worried or bothered.

clue.text: In some spots perhaps escape

definitions.meaning: to develop a rash of spots on the skin

explanation.definitionFit: A rash erupting on the skin and a jailbreak are both described by this phrasal verb.

clue.text: A shilling on the container makes you reel

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed above, so the coin comes before the container

parts.note: a bob was slang for a shilling, the old British coin worth twelve pence
a bin is a container

explanation.surface: Betting a shilling on a box leaves you staggering.
explanation.walkthrough: A bob was British slang for a shilling, a pre-decimal coin; 'reel' is not staggering but a spool.
explanation.definitionFit: A spool on which thread or yarn is wound is a reel.

clue.text: Regard French art and meet reverse.

parts.note: 'art' is the old second-person form of 'are'; in French 'tu es' is 'thou art', so es

indicators.note: the instruction to reverse tells us to read the word meet back to front

explanation.surface: Admire French artwork and an encounter turned round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'art' is not painting but the archaic verb 'thou art', French 'es'; 'reverse' turns MEET into TEEM.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold someone in high regard is to respect or value them, the same sense as the answer.

clue.text: Many eccentric ladies hand out the wrong cards

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a large number

indicators.note: eccentric means odd, so the letters of ladies are put into an odd order

explanation.surface: Lots of odd women dealing a bad hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' rearranges LADIES; 'Many' gives M, the Roman thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving players a faulty hand at the card table is a dealing error.

clue.text: Names bed perhaps in Hiram's Hospital

indicators.note: perhaps suggests these letters may be arranged some other way, an anagram signal

explanation.surface: Naming beds in a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges NAMES BED. Hiram's Hospital is the almshouse in Trollope's novel The Warden, home to twelve old pensioners.
explanation.definitionFit: The almshouse pensioners in Trollope's book are men who pray for their benefactor, the old term for such a beneficiary.

clue.text: "Only the actions of the just Smell —— " (Shirley)

definitions.text: "Only the actions of the just Smell —— " (Shirley)

parts.words: "Only the actions of the just Smell —— " (Shirley)
parts.note: James Shirley's poem 'The glories of our blood and state' ends with this line, completed 'and blossom in their dust'

explanation.surface: A line of seventeenth-century verse with its key word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: James Shirley's poem ends: 'Only the actions of the just / Smell sweet and blossom in their dust.'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word describes a pleasant fragrance, completing Shirley's line on good deeds.

clue.text: 13 has a setback, is reduced

parts.note: the answer to 13 across is a sailor, and AB, able-bodied seaman, is the abbreviation for one
read as two words, set back: the word set written backwards

explanation.surface: Someone suffers a reversal and is brought low.
explanation.walkthrough: Clue 13 is SEAMAN, so AB; it 'has' A plus 'setback', read as 'set' back, TES.
explanation.definitionFit: When a storm or fever dies down it lessens, the intransitive sense of the verb.

clue.text: Plum extractor

parts.note: in the nursery rhyme Little Jack Horner put a digit into his Christmas pie and pulled out a plum

explanation.surface: A tool for pitting fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme: 'He put in his thumb, and pulled out a plum.'
explanation.definitionFit: The short thick digit of the hand is what Jack Horner used to pull fruit from his pie.

clue.text: The compiler usually makes short work of it!

definitions.text: The compiler usually makes short work of it!

parts.words: The compiler usually makes short work of it!
parts.note: crossword setters habitually abbreviate this Latin word for a composition to OP, cutting it short

explanation.surface: The puzzle-setter dispatches this task quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes short work of' means dispatch quickly; read literally, setters shorten this word for a work to 'op'.
explanation.definitionFit: A numbered musical composition is a work, the Latin word for it.

clue.text: But this saga-woman was far from pacific!

definitions.text: But this saga-woman was far from pacific!

parts.words: But this saga-woman was far from pacific!
parts.note: the heroine of Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga, whose Greek name means peace, yet her story is full of strife

explanation.surface: A woman from a family saga who was anything but calm.
explanation.walkthrough: The name comes from Greek eirene, peace; the Forsyte heroine caused anything but peace in the family.
explanation.definitionFit: Soames Forsyte's wife in Galsworthy's novels bears a name derived from the Greek goddess of peace.

clue.text: Lucky to get work at the harbour with a French female

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a musical work
a port is a harbour
une is the French feminine form of 'a'

explanation.surface: Someone fortunate finds a job at the docks alongside a Frenchwoman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a French female' is not a woman but the feminine French article.
explanation.definitionFit: Something arriving at a fortunate moment is timely, close in sense to lucky.

clue.text: First prize in the rat-race ?

parts.note: the competitive scramble for success rewards winners with possessions that show off their rank, like a big car

explanation.surface: Asking what the winner of a rodent race receives.
explanation.walkthrough: The rat-race is the competitive struggle of working life; its prize is a possession that displays one's rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A flashy car or house is a badge displaying wealth and social standing, the reward that careerists chase.
